title: Psalm 70: Hurry, O LORD, to Help Me
summary: In five short verses a poor and needy person begs God to hurry to his rescue. He asks that those who seek his life be turned back in shame, and that all who seek God rejoice and say that God is great. The psalm ends where it began, with an urgent plea: do not delay.
story: Psalm 70 is nearly identical to Psalm 40:13-17, the closing prayer of a longer psalm in Book I. Here it stands on its own near the end of Book II, between the long lament of Psalm 69 and the lament of an aging believer in Psalm 71. Its brevity makes it one of the most portable prayers in Scripture, an emergency cry that can be said in a single breath. It also shows something about how the Psalter was assembled: songs and parts of songs were reused, adapted, and placed in new settings as Israel's worship grew.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. Of David. To bring remembrance.” The last phrase translates a Hebrew infinitive (lehazkir) that appears in a psalm heading only here and in Psalm 38. Its meaning is debated. Some connect it with the memorial portion of the grain offering, the part burned on the altar as a reminder before God (Leviticus 2:2), and think the psalm was sung when that offering was made. Others take it more generally: the psalm asks God to remember the one who prays, or it helps the worshiper bring his need to God's attention. As with other headings, Of David may mark authorship, a Davidic collection, or dedication, and scholars weigh it differently. Tradition reads the psalm as David's prayer in danger; the text itself names no event.

The relationship with Psalm 40 raises its own historical question. Most scholars think the lines existed first as part of Psalm 40 and were later lifted out for separate use, perhaps because a short plea for help was useful in worship. A minority argue the reverse, that this short prayer was older and was later joined to the thanksgiving of Psalm 40:1-12. Either way the two texts witness to a living tradition of prayer in which familiar words were reused.
cultural:
Shame and honor governed ancient social life. The speaker prays that his enemies be “ashamed and confounded” and “repelled and humiliated” (verse 2), which means publicly exposed as wrong and forced to retreat. The mocking cry in verse 3, “Aha, aha!”, is the gloating laugh of people who enjoy another's ruin. In a culture where one's standing before the community mattered enormously, such taunts cut deeply.

The self-description “poor and needy” (verse 5) was a familiar phrase in Israel's prayers. It can describe literal poverty, but it also names a posture before God: someone without resources, protectors, or influence, who depends on the LORD alone. Israel's law and prophets insisted that God himself defends the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner, so to call oneself poor and needy was to claim a place under that promise.
literary: The psalm is framed by urgency. It opens with two cries to hurry (verse 1) and closes with another hurry and do not delay (verse 5), so the plea for speed brackets everything. Between these, verses 2 and 3 pray against the enemies, and verse 4 prays for the faithful, setting two groups side by side: those who seek the speaker's life and those who seek God. The contrast is carefully balanced. The enemies say “Aha, aha!”; the faithful say “Let God be magnified!” The poem is a compact example of the lament form, with address, petition, a word about enemies, a word of confidence, and a final plea. Compared with Psalm 40:13-17, this version uses God (Elohim) in several places where Psalm 40 uses the LORD, a pattern typical of Psalms 42 to 83, which scholars call the Elohistic Psalter.

outline.t: Turn back those who seek my life
Let all who seek You rejoice
Poor and needy: do not delay

doctrines.note: Psalm 70 shows that short, urgent prayer is fully legitimate. The speaker does not argue at length or bargain; he names his need, names God as his help and deliverer, and asks for speed.
Salvation here is concrete rescue from enemies, and the faithful are described as “those who love Your salvation” (verse 4). They love not only being rescued but the God who rescues.

words.note: Chush, to hurry or hasten. It appears in verse 1 and again in verse 5 (together with a synonym), giving the psalm its note of urgency. The speaker doesn't doubt God can help; he fears help will come too late.

Ebyon, needy or poor. It often describes the person who has no human defender and must rely on God. In Israel's law and prophets, God pledges himself to the needy, so the speaker's confession of need is also a claim on God's promise.
Gadal, to be great or to magnify. In verse 4 the faithful cry that God be magnified, that is, acknowledged as great. It isn't that people add to God's size; they make his greatness known and visible.

christ: Psalm 70 is not quoted in the New Testament, and its connection with Jesus is thematic rather than predictive. Jesus lived as one of the poor and needy who trust God, and in his prayers in Gethsemane and on the cross he cried out to the Father in the same posture of dependence. Like the speaker, he was surrounded by people who gloated over his suffering and mocked his trust in God (Matthew 27:39-43). The psalm's contrast between those who seek to destroy and those who seek God, and its hope that the faithful will end in joy, find their fullest shape in the resurrection, where God answered the cry of his servant and vindicated him before his enemies.
questions: Psalm 70 is a prayer you could say in a moment of crisis. What short prayers do you turn to when you need help quickly?
The speaker calls himself poor and needy. What would it mean for you to come to God without pretending to have resources you don't have?
Verse 4 prays for all who seek God to rejoice. Why might a prayer for personal rescue include a prayer for other believers?
